title: THE OLD TESTAMENT MARRIAGE LAWS THAT MAKE CHRISTIANS UNCOMFORTABLE—AND THE JESUS-CENTERED TRUTH WE MISS WHEN WE READ THEM WRONG
paragraphs: THE OLD TESTAMENT MARRIAGE LAWS THAT MAKE CHRISTIANS UNCOMFORTABLE—AND THE JESUS-CENTERED TRUTH WE MISS WHEN WE READ THEM WRONG
Divorce. Captive women. Multiple wives. Broken homes. Laws that sound disturbing to modern ears. Did God approve of all of it—or is something far deeper happening in the pages we are tempted to skip?
There are passages in the Bible that almost nobody puts on a coffee mug.
Nobody decorates the nursery with them.
Nobody chooses them for the wedding invitation.
And sometimes, if we are painfully honest, we read them and quietly wonder...
God, why is this in Your Word?
A man gives his wife a certificate of divorce.
A soldier desires a woman captured in war.
A household contains more than one wife.
A vulnerable woman finds herself inside an ancient legal arrangement that feels painfully foreign to everything we know.
Then somebody who already doubts Christianity opens the Bible, points at one of those passages, and asks the question you were hoping they would never ask:
“So your God approves of this?”
And suddenly you feel trapped.
Defend the passage too quickly, and you may make God sound cruel.
Reject the passage because it makes you uncomfortable, and you place your feelings above Scripture.
Ignore it, and the question remains.
But there is another way.
The way Jesus Himself taught us to read.

And once you see it, some of the strangest marriage laws in the Old Testament begin telling a much larger story—not about God delighting in human brokenness, but about a holy God entering a brutally broken human world, restraining evil, protecting people within fallen circumstances, revealing His purposes progressively, and ultimately leading us toward the One who would bear human sin upon a cross.
Jesus Christ.
Before we go any further, remember this:
Not everything the Bible regulates is something the Bible celebrates.
That distinction changes everything.
The Bible records murder without endorsing murder.
It records adultery without blessing adultery.
It records polygamy without presenting polygamy as Eden's design.
It records slavery, warfare, betrayal, divorce, exploitation, family dysfunction, and terrible human decisions because Scripture does not airbrush humanity.
The Bible is brutally honest about us.
And that honesty begins almost immediately.
Before there were divorce certificates...
before Israel...
before Moses...
before kings accumulated wives...
before war fractured families...
there was a garden.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was God.
Genesis 2:24 describes the foundational pattern:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
One man.
One woman.
One covenant union.
One flesh.
Jesus later reaches backward through centuries of Israel's complicated marital history and deliberately brings His hearers back there.
Not first to Moses.
To creation.
When religious leaders questioned Him about divorce, Jesus answered by quoting Genesis and then declared:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
But they pushed Him.
Why, then, did Moses permit divorce?
And Jesus gave an answer that unlocks much of the tension Christians experience when reading Old Testament marriage legislation:
“Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so.”
Read those words again.
From the beginning it was not so.
Jesus distinguishes between God's creational design and a concession operating within human hardness.
That matters enormously.
The Greek expression translated “hardness of heart” is σκληροκαρδία — sklērokardia.
A hard heart.
A stubborn heart.
A heart resistant to God's intention.
Jesus does not say divorce existed because God's ideal marriage needed improvement.
He points to human sin.
That means some Old Testament laws must be understood not as photographs of Eden restored, but as God's legislation addressing people living east of Eden.
There is a difference between God creating an ideal and God regulating damage after humans abandon that ideal.
Imagine an emergency room.
A surgeon treating a gunshot wound is not endorsing gunshot wounds.
The treatment exists because something has gone terribly wrong.
In a similar way, biblical law sometimes meets human beings inside circumstances already twisted by sin and places boundaries around what fallen people are doing.
Consider Deuteronomy 24.
The Hebrew text speaks of a סֵפֶר כְּרִיתֻת — sefer keritut, literally a written document or “certificate of cutting off,” a certificate of divorce.
Modern readers sometimes approach the passage as though God is enthusiastically introducing divorce.
But Jesus refuses that reading.
The legislation addresses a situation in which divorce is already occurring and establishes legal boundaries around what follows.
And notice something easy to miss.
The woman is not merely an object endlessly transferable between men.
Once divorced and subsequently married to another man, the first husband cannot simply reclaim her later after that second marriage ends.
A boundary has been drawn.
The law restrains the former husband.
The woman cannot simply be treated as property that can be passed out, reclaimed, and recycled according to male convenience.
Does that mean Deuteronomy 24 represents the fullness of God's vision for marriage?
Jesus says no.
“From the beginning it was not so.”
But does that mean the law is meaningless or morally embarrassing?
Again, no.
It reveals God governing a fallen society while still pointing beyond that society toward His original intention.
And then we arrive at one of the passages that can make modern Christians deeply uncomfortable.
Deuteronomy 21:10–14.
A woman has been taken captive in warfare.
A victorious Israelite soldier finds her attractive.
At first glance, the power imbalance is horrifying.
She has lost.
Her world has collapsed.
Perhaps her family is gone.
Perhaps everything familiar has disappeared.
She is vulnerable.
So what does God's law do?
It does not allow the soldier simply to seize her sexually in the heat of conquest.
There is a process.
She enters the household.
She receives time to mourn her father and mother.
A full month.
Her grief is acknowledged.
If the relationship later ends, the man is forbidden to sell her.
He cannot turn her into merchandise.
He must release her.
The text explicitly forbids treating her as something to be sold after what has happened.
Does that erase every moral difficulty modern readers feel when encountering an ancient warfare text?
No.
We should not pretend that it does.
Faithfulness to Scripture does not require pretending difficult passages are easy.
But neither should we commit the opposite mistake: reading an ancient law as though its purpose were to create the broken situation it is actually regulating.
The law enters a world where defeated women could be extraordinarily vulnerable and places restrictions on the victorious man.
His power is not absolute.
His desire is not absolute.
Her humanity cannot simply disappear because he won a battle.
That pattern appears elsewhere.
Exodus 21:7–11 addresses another ancient arrangement involving an economically vulnerable woman. Again, modern readers understandably recoil at the social institution surrounding the text.
But look carefully at what the law requires.
If the man takes another wife, he may not deprive the first woman of food, clothing, or marital provision.
And if he refuses those obligations?
She goes free.
Without paying him.
In other words, the law places obligations upon the socially powerful and provides consequences when those obligations are violated.
That does not mean Christians should resurrect Israel's ancient civil arrangements.
It means we must learn to ask the right interpretive question.
Not merely:
“Why does this situation exist in the Bible?”
But:
“What is God's law doing inside this already-existing fallen situation?”
That question changes the landscape.
And then there is polygamy.
Abraham.
Jacob.
David.
Solomon.
Men associated with enormous moments in redemptive history had multiple wives.
So did God design marriage that way?
Look at the stories.
Really look.
The Bible rarely needs to interrupt the narrative and scream, “THIS IS GOING BADLY.”
The consequences tell you.
Sarah and Hagar.
Pain.
Jealousy.
Abraham caught between households.
Jacob, Leah, and Rachel.
Competition.
Tears.
Favoritism.
Children growing up inside rivalry.
Then David.
Then Solomon, whose many wives ultimately helped turn his heart toward other gods.
Scripture does not hide the wreckage.
Sometimes the Bible condemns sin through direct command.
Sometimes it lets you stand inside the burning house long enough to smell the smoke.
The existence of polygamous men in Scripture is no more proof that polygamy represents God's ideal than David's adultery proves adultery represents God's ideal.
The heroes of Scripture are not the Hero of Scripture.
That distinction may save someone's faith.
Abraham is not Jesus.
Moses is not Jesus.
David is not Jesus.
Solomon is not Jesus.
They are sinners standing inside the same story of redemption that eventually reaches us.
And this is where everything begins moving toward the cross.
Because biblical marriage is ultimately bigger than marriage.
The prophets describe covenant faithfulness between God and His people.
Malachi calls a wife אֵשֶׁת בְּרִיתֶךָ — eshet beritekha, “the wife of your covenant.”
Marriage is not merely possession.
Not merely sexuality.
Not merely social convenience.
Covenant.
Faithfulness.
Loyalty.
Love that keeps its word.
Then the New Testament opens something breathtaking.
Paul writes:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.
“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.”
Ephesians 5:25.
Notice the command.
ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate.
Love.
And what defines that love?
Christ.
Not domination.
Not selfish entitlement.
Not “I am the man, therefore I get whatever I want.”
Christ.
And what did Christ do?
ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν — heauton paredōken.
“He gave Himself up.”
Suddenly biblical authority in marriage cannot honestly be interpreted through selfish male privilege.
The Husband-pattern is a crucified Savior.
The model is Jesus giving Himself.
Bleeding.
Serving.
Sacrificing.
Seeking the holiness and good of His bride.
The cross turns worldly power upside down.
The world says:
“If you have power, make people sacrifice for you.”
Jesus says:
“If you love, give yourself.”
And perhaps this is where the Old Testament marriage laws stop being merely an intellectual problem and become painfully personal.
Because it is easy to analyze ancient Israel.
Harder to analyze our own hearts.
You may never hand someone a Hebrew sefer keritut.
But have you emotionally abandoned the person you promised to love?
You may never have multiple wives like Solomon.
But have you allowed another person, fantasy, addiction, ambition, secret conversation, pornography, resentment, or hidden desire to occupy a place in your heart that belongs inside your covenant?
You may never live under ancient Israelite household legislation.
But have you ever used power selfishly?
Manipulated somebody who trusted you?
Demanded submission while refusing sacrifice?
Quoted Scripture to win an argument while refusing to resemble Jesus?
Suddenly the ancient text is no longer sitting safely three thousand years away.
It has walked into the room.
And now it is looking at us.
Somebody reading this has been wounded by marriage.
Somebody was abandoned.
Somebody was betrayed.
Somebody stayed awake while their spouse slept beside them, wondering how two people sharing one mattress could somehow feel thousands of miles apart.
Somebody begged God to restore a marriage that still collapsed.
Somebody carries shame because they were the one who destroyed it.
Somebody committed adultery.
Somebody lied.
Somebody left.
Somebody became cold.
Somebody is divorced and still feels as though the word has been tattooed across their forehead.
Somebody thinks their past permanently disqualifies them from being deeply loved by God.
And this is where Christianity becomes more than an argument about ancient law.
Because Jesus did not come merely to explain Moses.
Jesus came to save sinners.
The same Jesus who reaffirmed the seriousness of marriage also sat near a well speaking with a woman whose relational history was shattered.
Five husbands.
And the man she currently had was not her husband.
Jesus knew.
Every chapter.
Every relationship.
Every regret.
Every whispered accusation.
Every failure.
He knew.
And He stayed.
He spoke truth without pretending her life was whole.
But He did not reduce her to her scandal.
He offered living water.
That is Jesus.
Truth without cruelty.
Grace without pretending sin does not matter.
Holiness without hopelessness.
Conviction without abandonment.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross says your sin was so serious that Christ died.
But the resurrection says your sin does not have to write the final sentence.
Maybe your marriage story is beautiful.
Thank God.
Protect it.
Maybe your marriage is wounded.
Seek Christ, wisdom, prayer, biblical counsel, repentance, safety where necessary, forgiveness where appropriate, and help from mature believers.
Maybe your marriage ended.
Do not rewrite Scripture to make sin harmless.
But do not rewrite the Gospel to make grace powerless either.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Jesus sees you.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Repent.
Not performative regret.
Not excuses.
Not “I made mistakes.”
Repentance.
Bring the ugliness into the light.
Christ's blood is not reserved for respectable sinners.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is why Christians should never read Old Testament marriage laws merely asking, “Which ancient regulations do I copy?”
We read them within the whole biblical story.
Creation tells us the design.
The fall tells us why relationships fracture.
The law shows God confronting and restraining sin among a covenant people in an ancient world.
The prophets deepen the language of covenant faithfulness.
Jesus takes us back to creation and exposes hardness of heart.
The apostles show marriage illuminated by Christ and His Church.
And the Gospel tells sinners where shattered covenant-breakers can finally find mercy.
At the cross.
The Bible begins with a marriage in a garden.
And near its end, Revelation gives us the marriage supper of the Lamb.
Do you see the thread?
Marriage was never merely about us.
Human marriage is temporary.
Christ and His redeemed people are forever.
Every faithful Christian marriage is meant to whisper something about that greater covenant.
Every broken marriage reminds us how desperately humanity needs redemption.
Every repentant sinner restored by Christ becomes evidence that failure does not have sovereign authority over the future.
Jesus does.
This is why we must stop weaponizing difficult Old Testament passages.
And we must stop being ashamed of them too.
Read them carefully.
Read historically.
Read grammatically.
Read covenantally.
Read canonically.
Read them through what Jesus Himself reveals about God's intention.
Do not flatten every biblical law into the same category.
Do not confuse description with prescription.
Do not confuse regulation with celebration.
Do not isolate Moses from Genesis.
Do not isolate Genesis from Jesus.
And never isolate any difficult biblical passage from the great redemptive story reaching its climax in Christ crucified and risen.
Because when Scripture exposes human hardness, the answer is not pretending humanity was never hard.
The answer is a Savior who can give us new hearts.
Maybe that is the part we resist.
We want God to explain everyone else's brokenness.
God wants to confront ours.
We want to discuss ancient husbands.
Jesus asks what kind of husband you are.
We want to discuss ancient wives.
Jesus asks whether you have been faithful.
We want to debate Moses.
Jesus asks whether our hearts are hard.
And suddenly this article isn't about “those strange Old Testament marriage laws” anymore.
It is about you.
Me.
Our excuses.
Our wounds.
Our lust.
Our selfishness.
Our marriages.
Our divorces.
Our secrets.
Our covenant-breaking hearts.
And a crucified King standing before sinners with scarred hands.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to write your whole story publicly.
But maybe you need to stop pretending.

And if you once thought these Old Testament passages proved God did not care about vulnerable people, but now you want to study Scripture more carefully, say so. Honest questions are better than borrowed answers.
Someone on your Facebook friends list is quietly wrestling with these exact passages.
Someone thinks Christianity cannot answer them.
Someone has been wounded by a church leader who used biblical marriage language to justify selfishness, control, or abuse.
Someone divorced years ago and still wonders whether Jesus wants them anywhere near Him.
Difficult passages rarely become easy after one reading, and someday someone may ask you the question this article just helped you face.

If you genuinely want your resources to glorify God, then steward them prayerfully. Support faithful Gospel work where the Lord leads you. Share biblical truth instead of merely consuming it. Help put Scripture in front of people who may never walk voluntarily into a church.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the exhausted Christian.
Invite the lukewarm believer who knows something has gone cold.
Invite the skeptic who still has questions.
Invite the person recovering from divorce.
Invite the husband who needs to rediscover sacrificial love.
Invite the wife who feels unseen.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks the Bible has nothing meaningful to say to a modern world.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's approval.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot share enough Christian posts to erase your sins.
You cannot purchase redemption.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Christianity's invitation has never ultimately been:
“Become impressive.”
It is:
“Come to Christ.”
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Him.
And let the One who carried your sin begin rewriting everything your sin tried to destroy.
Because perhaps the most shocking thing about the Bible's broken marriages is not that God allowed their ugly stories to remain on the page.
Perhaps the most shocking thing is that He kept pursuing broken people through them...
until the story reached a cross...
an empty tomb...
and a Bridegroom who gave Himself to redeem a bride who could never rescue herself.
So when you encounter those uncomfortable Old Testament marriage laws again, do not run from the page.
Look closer.
Behind the divorce certificates, fractured households, human hardness, compromised men, vulnerable women, covenant failures, tears, and consequences is a story moving relentlessly toward Jesus.
And maybe your own story feels scandalous right now.
Maybe there are chapters you wish could be ripped out.
Maybe your family knows.
Maybe nobody knows.
Jesus does.
Your scandal may explain where you have been.
It does not possess the authority to decide who Christ can make you become.
The pages you are most ashamed of may become the very pages where future generations discover how fiercely Jesus saves.
